title: Gaming Consoles Part 3: Nintendo - [Business Breakdowns, EP.203]
thesis: This episode argues that Nintendo is successfully monetizing its world-class IP through movies, theme parks, and other entertainment ventures, generating significant standalone profits outside its core video game business. It highlights Nintendo's strong balance sheet, history of buybacks, and focus on the long-term permanence of its franchises as key strengths, while noting the primary risk is that recent transformational progress could unwind.

claims.claim: Nintendo is properly monetizing its world-class IP through movies and theme parks, unlike Disney which destroyed its franchises.
claims.quote: But essentially Nintendo has confirmed that not only was the movie not a one-off, But since then, they've released that the sequel Super Mario Bros. 2 comes out in early 2006. They've announced a new motion cap Zelda movie, but there are many more in the works.

claims.claim: Nintendo's IP entertainment division is a standalone profit engine worth between 50 to 20 billion in and of itself outside of the core video game business.
claims.quote: Obviously, not only is it a good standalone new pillar of profits or earnings engine for the company, but there are network effects. The more people that see the movie and get familiarized with Nintendo's IP and characters, all the more are likely to go purchase its video game hardware and software.

claims.claim: Mario titles increased roughly 50% in total sales in the aftermath of the Super Mario brother movie.
claims.quote: And you saw that. I think Mario titles increased roughly 50% in total sales in the aftermath of the Super Mario brother movie. So, again, it's a great business. I think it's probably worth somewhere between a third to half what you're paying for Nintendo in its entire Gives of day.

claims.claim: Nintendo is properly monetizing its world-class IP in ways it wasn't historically willing to do, and takes its devotion to its IP and the permanence of its franchises very seriously.
claims.quote: But they take their devotion to their IP and the permanence of their are deadly seriously. And ensuring that it is at that qualitative threshold to be released and to grow the value of the franchise is pretty much everything. And I'll give be an example of how hardcore Nintendo is about this stuff.

claims.claim: Nintendo is very much focused on a middle way where they take the permanence of their art and the care of these franchises they have built up over the last 40 years very seriously.
claims.quote: And you're not going to see the cash grabs or injecting contemporary politics into escapism or any of the other unforced airs you've seen at Disney. that has, frankly, permanently impaired some of the best IP in the world. You're absolutely not going to see that at Nintendo.

claims.claim: In the last 10 years, Nintendo has bought back roughly 11% of their equity in various bits and pieces.
claims.quote: In the last 10 years, they've bought back roughly 11% of their equity in various bits and pieces. But that has stopped, I'd say, over the last two years, as they have been moving towards the first major iterative upgrade transition of their hardware with the Switch 2.

claims.claim: Nintendo has a huge balance sheet with cash and diversified by currency or all of its hidden balance sheet assets, and the cash will start to pile up so fast that they'll really have no other choice but to start returning it in droves, mostly through buybacks, but through continuously increasing dividends as well.
claims.quote: when you have a balance sheet or a war chest as huge as Nintendo has, whether you're talking about just cash and diversified by currency or all of its hidden balance sheet assets, the cash will start to pile up so fast that they'll really have no other choice but to start returning it in droves, mostly through buybacks, but through continuously increasing dividends as well.

claims.claim: The biggest risk by far is that all of the immense transformational progress seen over the last seven, eight years starts to unwind and creep back the other way.
claims.quote: The risk is very simply that they start to unwind all of the progress that they have made since 2015. They resort to becoming insular again and guarding their IP and they stop making movies. They stop expanding on the theme parks. They stop using their excess cash in value-accretive shareholder-friendly ways.
